findings.text: Swift: `#"""` always opens a multi-line raw string. Swift's lexer instead reads `#"""` as a single-line raw string when its closer (`"#`) follows on the same line, as in `let q = #"""#` (a one-quote string) or `#""""#`. Here the opener takes `"""#` as its closer, so the rest of that line and the lines after it count as code inside a string until a `"""#` turns up. Comment lines in between are miscounted.

The char-literal escape and Unicode cases on lines 185–186 (`'\''`, `'\\'`, `'\n'`, `'\u{1F600}'`, `'😀'`) prove nothing. No `"` or `/*` follows them on their lines, so dropping the escape or `u`-flag alternatives from the char regex still passes the test. Only `'"'` (line 184) and the `'static` before `/* a` (line 187) actually test the char-literal rule. Put a `"` or `/*` after each case so a misread would carry over to the next line.

`let bar"x";` is meant to check that `bar"` opens a plain string, not a raw `r"`. Raw and plain strings both close at the second `"` here, so removing the `(?<!\w)` lookbehind still passes. It needs an escape that only a plain string honours, e.g. `let bar"\"/*";` followed by a comment line.

The Swift raw-string escape rule is never really checked. On line 222, `\"#` closes or doesn't, but the `// a comment` after it is on the same code line, so treating `\` as an escape still passes. The case where the rule matters, a backslash before the closer of a multi-line `#"""` string (e.g. a line `\"""#`), is not tested. Line 253 has the same problem for Lua escapes: `"a \" -- b"` is code either way.

The goal says Rust byte strings `b"…"`, `br"…"` and `br#"…"#` may span lines. The test only has single-line byte strings (`br#"x\"#;`, `b"/*"`), so a regression in multi-line byte strings, such as `[bc]?` being dropped from the raw-string regex, would go unnoticed.

blind.summary: I found no blockers and no major bugs. The Rust, Swift and Lua handling matches the goal for every case it names, and other languages behave as before. I traced every test by hand; I did not run them. Four things are worth fixing. One is a small Swift lexing gap: the single-line raw strings `#"""#` and `#""""#` are read as multi-line strings. The other three are tests that do not check what they claim: several assertions would still pass if the escape, lifetime-lookbehind or raw-escape logic were removed, and multi-line byte strings are never tested.
